principles.text: There are thousands of valid ways to trade and no single model answer - find the style that suits your personality, risk appetite, and character, and don't copy someone else's wholesale.
Managing longs and shorts simultaneously can mess with your mind; if it does, it is easier and simpler to focus on one side of the market at a time.
Size shorts exactly like longs: position size is derived purely from stop width and the fixed amount of capital you are willing to risk per trade.
Don't put a timer on study - value the process over the result. How you approach and drill a problem matters more than whether you reach a conclusion this time.
Replay historical periods side by side (e.g. long AMD while short Square in late 2021) to train your eyes on market dynamics and test whether an approach could work for you.
Do your own study to make knowledge yours - you can take ideas from others' sharing, but you have to verify everything yourself; the market leaves puzzles in the charts for you to discover.
After a stretched, high-volume uptrend, a failed breakout at the prior swing high that builds the first lower high marks the end of the uptrend the vast majority of the time (he estimates ~98-99%).
Price respects unfilled gaps quite efficiently - use prior unfilled gaps as support/resistance levels for entries and targets.

Check the sector/theme before the stock: short weak stocks in weak sectors (never a laggard in a strong sector), and go long where many peers in the theme show strength. Then work top-down: theme, weekly, daily, intraday.
Short broken-down leaders on the first bounce or first pullback into the declining 9/50 EMA, ideally where it confluences with prior swing lows and the declining weekly 9.

To time a short intraday, wait for the 5-minute candle to lose momentum, then drop to the 1-minute chart and use the anchored VWAP from the open (or high of day) for the entry - it works beyond parabolic shorts.
Always hunt for entry tactics that tighten the stop - a tighter, logical stop is what maximizes risk/reward per trade (vs e.g. a 2% stop from a 5-minute breakdown).
Candlestick pattern names are gimmicks - the same chart can read bullish (e.g. morning star) in isolation; context of theme, extension, and volume decides the trade, not the pattern.
Cover shorts into weakness rather than trailing all the way down: the faster the flush, the more you cover; if price drifts down slowly and orderly, trail longer.
Cover short positions before the company's earnings rather than holding through the event.

Only take a mean-reversion long after a genuine panic flush - one huge red candle undercutting all support (e.g. into the weekly 21 EMA). If the decline is slow and orderly with no panic, skip it; the base needs more time.
Don't buy a stock showing relative weakness / lagging the market, especially after a quick huge-volume correction from the top of its last push higher.
There is no certainty in markets, only probability - anyone who tells you something is definitely going up or down is a scammer.

After a sector runs hot and a name is already up ~250% in 3 months with peers rolling over, the odds of another 100% leg are low - most of the buying power has been consumed by the run and the late gap-ups.

Your own trade feedback is the best market indicator: in a strong market even bad entries get rewarded, but when even good entries get stopped out - a losing streak of 10-20 - the market has turned unfavorable to your style.

Tight stops raise your trade frequency, which gives you more and timelier feedback from the market - consecutive stop-outs are a useful signal, not just a cost, if you act on them instead of spiraling.

He cut risk per trade from 0.5% to 0.3% (sometimes less) this year to control drawdowns; tight stops still produce solid position sizes, and a higher number of entries compensates for the smaller unit risk.
If you are in a drawdown and don't know what you're doing, stop trading for a while and take a rest.
In a middle-of-the-range market with no clear direction, there is no need to push - and don't get influenced by social-media noise, FOMO, or panic.
Superior returns require luck (a market that cooperates with your style) plus a tight-stop approach that maximizes risk/reward - don't expect top-decile results in a choppy, weak uptrend.
